Recog 1.001`$P->P . P  .: P`=This is a perfectly correct application of MP.  The fact that the rule is stated using distinct antecedent and consequent allows the antecedent and consequent to be distinct, but does not require it.`&Recog 1.001`C
Recog 1.002`$~T->(T->U) . ~(T->U)  .: ~~T `=Note that the conclusion must be as given, and cannot be "T", which is not the negation of the antecedent of the conditional.`&Recog 1.002`C
Recog 1.003`$W->X . ~X  .: ~W`=Recog 1.003`CW`*
Recog 1.005`$~Q->~R . R  .: Q`=The second premise is not the negation of the consequent of the conditional (as is required), and the conclusion is not the negation of the antecedent of the conditional (as is also required).  The result can be obtained from those two premises, but not directly by a single application of MT.  Rather, one must first apply DN to the second premise, then apply MT to obtain \l"~~Q"\l, then apply a second DN to that result.`&Recog 1.005`C
Recog 1.006`$~~~Z  .: ~Z`=Recog 1.006`C
Recog 1.007`$(~Q->S)->P . ~Q->S  .: P `=Note that the "official" outermost parentheses have been dropped in the second premise, but cannot be dropped in the first premise.`&Recog 1.007`CW`*
Recog 1.008`$~~P  .: ~~P`=Recog 1.008`C
Recog 1.009`$~~P->~Q . ~~Q  .: ~P`=This case is rather like 1.005.  Although MT can be applied directly to these premises, it yields \l"~~~P"\l rather than \l"~P"\l.  The latter requires an application of DN.`&Recog 1.009`C
Recog 1.010`$T->S  .: ~~(T->S)`=As in 1.007, the "official" outermost parentheses have been dropped in the premise, but cannot be dropped in the conclusion.`&Recog 1.010`C
Recog 1.012`$~(R->T)->U . ~~U  .: ~~(R->T) `=One too many negations in the second premise.`&Recog 1.012`C
Recog 1.013`$T . T->~Q  .: ~Q`=Note that the order in which the premises appear does not matter.`&Recog 1.013`C
Recog 1.014`$~~~P->Q  .: ~P->Q`=If we restore the dropped parentheses, we will see that the premise is \l"(~~~P->Q)"\l, not \l"~~~(P->Q)"\l, and thus a conditional, not a negation.  Perhaps this is an attempt to apply the rule of DN to just the antecedent of the conditional, the \l"~~~P"\l part.  But rules may never be applied to the interior of a formula.  (Only when the derived rule of Interchange of Equivalents is established will any rules become applicable to the interior of formulas.)`&Recog 1.014`C
Recog 1.015`$~(R->~S)->(~P->~T) . ~(~P->~T)  .: ~~(R->~S)`=Recog 1.015`CW`*
Recog 1.016`$P->Y  .: P->Y`=One may wonder about the utility of the rule R.  Its most common use is to bring a line required for boxing and canceling down below the Show line that is to be canceled.  In theory, this rule is dispensable, in the sense that any derivation that uses it can be transformed into a derivation that does not use it.`&Recog 1.016`C
Recog 1.017`$(P->Q)->~~S  .: (P->Q)->S `=This failed attempt to apply DN violates the Prime Directive:  Rules may never be applied to the interior of a formula.`&Recog 1.017`C
Recog 1.019`$R->Q  .: ~~R->Q`=Compare 1.014.  The premise, in official notation, is \l"(R->Q)"\l; the conclusion is \l"(~~R->Q)"\l.  This is not a correct application of DN.`&Recog 1.019`CW`*
Recog 1.020`$(P->T)->(R->(S->P)) . (P->T) . R  .: S->P`=The conclusion can be obtained by two applications of MP, the first to premises 1 and 2, the second to the result and premise 3, but it cannot be obtained by a single application of MP.  Using queuing, a correct justification for the conclusion would read, "PR1 PR2 MP PR3 MP".`&Recog 1.020`C
Recog 2.001`$~(P&Q)  .: ~Q`=This appears to be another attempt to apply an inference rule, here, Simplification, to the interior of a formula (see explanations of answers to problems 1.014 and 1.017 of Chapter I).\nRULES MAY NEVER BE APPLIED TO THE INTERIOR OF A FORMULA.\n(Only when the derived rule of Interchange of Equivalents is established will any rules become applicable to the interior of formulas.)`&Recog 2.001`C
Recog 2.002`$~(P|Q)&((R->~P)<->S)  .: ~(P|Q) `=In Command Mode, one can avoid a query by directly citing the form of the rule, here, Simplification on the left, or SL.`&Recog 2.002`C
Recog 2.003`$~P&Q->R  .: ~P`=The attempt to Simplify reflect an incorrect parsing of the premise, which is correctly parsed as a conditional \l"((~P&Q)->R)"\l not a conjunction.`&Recog 2.003`CW`*
Recog 2.004`$~S|R . P->Q  .: (P->Q)&(~S|R)`=Note that both pairs of parentheses are required in the conclusion; the first by the fact that \l"->"\l is a major connective, the second by the fact that \l"&"\l and \l"|"\l are both minor connectives.`&Recog 2.004`C
Recog 2.006`$(R|S) . Q<->P  .: (R|S)&Q<->P`=This attempt to apply ADJ fails because the conclusion is a biconditional (the major connective as between \l"&"\l and \l"<->"\l).  If the conclusion had been written \l"(R|S)&(Q<->P)"\l, it would have been a correct application of ADJ.`&Recog 2.006`C
Recog 2.007`$~P . ~(Q<->R)  .: ~(P&(Q<->R)) `=Perhaps the perpetrator of this argument thought to hold the negations in abeyance while adjoining the negated formulas, then carry down the negation.`&Recog 2.007`CW`*
Recog 2.008`$P->Q  .: P->Q|R`=Like 1.006, this attempt at Addition miscarries because of the lack of parentheses in the conclusion.  A correct application of ADD (more precisely ADDR) would yield \l"(P->Q)|R"\l.`&Recog 2.008`C
Recog 2.009`$R&S  .: Q|(R&S)`=For this correct application of Addition on the Left using the parameter "Q" for the formula to be added, one could simply enter "PR1 ADDL/Q".  In Command Mode, no queries would result.`&Recog 2.009`C
Recog 2.010`$R->S  .: (R->S)|(S->Q)`=As in 2.009, a Command Mode command of \l"PR1 ADDR/(S->Q)"\l would generate the line without queries.  Note that when using parameters, even \l "PR1 ADDR/S->Q"\l will generate the correct line.`&Recog 2.010`C
Recog 2.011`$P&~Q  .: (P|Q)&(~Q|R)`=This doesn't begin to be derivable by the application of a single primitive rule.  However, the following single command, queued and with parameters, will generate the line: "PR1 SL ADDR/Q PR1 SR ADDR/R ADJ".`&Recog 2.011`CW`*
Recog 2.013`$P|Q  .: R|P|Q`=As in 2.012, our conventions for dropping parentheses allows them to be dropped for a series of disjuncts only if the disjuncts are associated to the left.  Hence, the conclusion, in official notation, is \l"((R|P)|Q)"\l.  This formula is not directly derivable from \l"(P|Q)"\l by Addition.  Only \l"(R|(P|Q))"\l follows directly by ADD.  In order to get the conclusion as it appears, one must then use the Derived Rule of Assoc (or derive the appropriate instance of T54).`&Recog 2.013`C
Recog 2.014`$~(R|S)|(P->S) . ~(P->S)  .: ~(R|S)`=Recog 2.014`C
Recog 2.015`$P|~(Q&R) . ~P  .:Q&R`=What happened to the negation? This failed attempt at MTP should have had as its conclusion \l"~(Q&R)"\l.`&Recog 2.015`CW`*
Recog 2.016`$P|~(S->(T|R)) . ~P  .: ~(S->(T|R))`=Note that MTP applies equally to either the left disjunct or the right disjunct (compare 2.014).`&Recog 2.016`C
Recog 2.017`$(P|Q)->R . ~P  .: Q `=One can't just ignore the \l"->R"\l.`&Recog 2.017`C
Recog 2.018`$~(P<->Q)  .: ~(P->Q)`=Shame shame! Again, an attempt to apply BC to the interior of a formula (see 2.001).`&Recog 2.018`C
Recog 2.020`$P<->Q&R  .: Q->P`=That old devil parsing has blinded the perpetrator.  The premise is indeed a biconditional, \l"(P<->(Q&R))"\l, but the BCR would yield \l"Q&R->P"\l, not \l"Q->P"\l.`&Recog 2.020`C
Recog 2.021`$P&Q->R . R->P&Q  .: R<->P&Q`=The biconditional in either direction can be derived from these two premises.`&Recog 2.021`C
Recog 2.022`$(P->Q)->R . R->(Q->P)  .: R<->(P<->Q) `=This is a sly one.  The \l"(P->Q)"\l gets reversed in the second premise.  The second premise needed to be \l"R->(P->Q)"\l to validly yield any conclusion by CB, and even then it wouldn't yield this conclusion.  (What would it yield?)`&Recog 2.022`C
Recog 2.023`$(S|~R)->R . R->(S|~R)  .: (S|~R)<->R`=Recog 2.023`CW`*
Recog 3.001`$@x(Fx->Gy)  .: Fx->Gy`=The instantial term is the variable "x" itself.  In the conclusion, the outermost parentheses were dropped in accordance with the conventions.`&Recog 3.001`C
Recog 3.002`$!xFx  .: Fi`=EI, but only on the assumption that that the external constraint is satisfied, namely that the instantial variable "i" has no prior occurrence anywhere in the derivation.`&Recog 3.002`C
Recog 3.004`$!yGy  .: Ga `=In EI, the instantial term must be a variable; "a" is a name letter, not a variable.`&Recog 3.004`CW`*
Recog 3.005`$@xGy  .: Gy`=The quantifier phrase is vacuous; it binds nothing.  You may wonder what the instantial term is.  Let it be any term, say "a". If we replace all the occurrences of "x" that are bound by the vacuous quantifier, then since there are no such occurrences, we change nothing.`&Recog 3.005`C
Recog 3.006`$!xGy  .: Gi`=As in 3.005, the quantifier phrase is vacuous.  Therefore any application of EI would yield "Gy", not "Gi".`&Recog 3.006`C
